extracted.intended_audience: writers preparing book-length manuscripts (fiction and nonfiction) for developmental editing
extracted.subtask_description: A practical checklist and set of evaluative criteria for preparing, commissioning, and carrying out a developmental edit of a book-length manuscript (fiction or nonfiction), including setup, structure, pacing, character/voice, worldbuilding, market fit and revision planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define your goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick one primary aim and two secondary aims (e.g., structure, character or thesis clarity, pacing, market fit). Write one sentence for each aim and use these as the lens for all notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Structure — Do scenes and chapters build in a clear causal chain. Character or thesis clarity — Do motivations make sense. Pacing — Where does energy drop. Market fit — Does the book meet core reader expectations for the genre. Tape the sentences where you work; every note should serve those aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a briefing pack
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short, skimmable pack for the editor including a 1–2 page synopsis (spoilers included), a chapter outline, a cast or key concepts list, a short author bio, and a mini exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it short and easy to skim. Outline: chapter list with one line per chapter or reverse outline (purpose, conflict, change). Cast: roles, wants, ages for fiction; core concepts and the problem each solves for nonfiction. Mini exercise: write the whole book in 300 words in 20 minutes to expose gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify audience and comps
rubrics_metrics.description: Name the primary reader in one line (age, interests, what they hope to gain) and pick 3–5 comparable titles from the last five years; state what readers of each comp expect and how your book delivers or differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish the sentence for each comp: 'Readers who loved [Title] will expect [feature]. My book delivers [version of that feature] and differs in [one meaningful way].' Examples provided for fiction and nonfiction to show how to map expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Define practical constraints like target word count by genre, must-keep elements, deal-breakers, timeline, and publishing path to guide revision choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: target word counts by genre (romance 70–90k, thrillers 60–80k, epic fantasy 90–120k, prescriptive nonfiction 50–70k, memoir 70–90k). List non-negotiables (e.g., dual timeline) and deal-breakers (topics/portrayals to avoid). Record timeline and whether trade or self-publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare working files and style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the manuscript easy to read and mark up: single .docx with chapters on new pages, 12pt double-spaced, clear scene-break markers, consistent styles, Track Changes enabled, and a one-page style sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style sheet should include names, spellings, place names, hyphenation, numbers rules, spelling choice (UK/US), formatting choices (ellipses, dashes), and be updated during revision. Use one Heading style for chapter titles and avoid manual formatting tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the right questions to guide the edit
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick five big, open questions (one primary aim + two secondary aims recommended) to focus the editor's attention on strategic issues rather than nitty-gritty line edits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction examples: 'Where does the story sag?' 'Does the protagonist drive the plot through choices?' Nonfiction examples: 'Is the thesis simple and bold?' 'Does each chapter advance the argument without repeats?' Add one open slot for surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide scope and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree on level of review (full manuscript vs partial), deliverables (editorial letter vs letter + margin notes), meetings (kick-off, debrief), rechecks, and timeline before work starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial review common for early structure checks (e.g., opening 50 pages + synopsis). Define whether margin notes will use Track Changes. Agree on recheck scope and timing to avoid scope creep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core promise (one-line promise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Name the book's promise in one sentence — premise or thesis plus the reader's expected change or outcome — and use it as the test for every chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction template: 'A [character] must [goal] before [ticking threat], or [cost].' Nonfiction template: 'This book helps [reader] achieve [outcome] by [method].' Test on a friend: if they respond 'I want that,' the hook holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro architecture / major beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the manuscript follows a clear shape with named major beats and a causal chain between them (inciting incident, midpoint reversal, crisis, climax, resolution for fiction; logical table of contents and progressive learning for nonfiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mini exercises: write a one-line beat sheet (five lines for fiction) or one line per chapter for nonfiction. Check causality: scenes should trigger one another rather than feel episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throughlines (track core threads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track central throughlines—goal, motivation, conflict, alignment—and ensure subplots or supporting pillars pressure or support the central story/argument rather than distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a quick grid or color-code manuscript: one color for the central goal, others for subplots/support pillars. Drop or fold any subplot that doesn't complicate or advance the central scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every turn should raise consequences; escalation should come from choices and set-ups should pay off, with the middle increasing pressure rather than padding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction: personal, social and public stakes should climb; reversals should come from choices. Nonfiction: each chapter should answer a new question and introduce a tougher one. Add margin notes: 'Because of this, the next chapter must address X.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain chronological consistency—track dates, seasons, scenes per day, ages, travel times, injuries, and institutional calendars—to avoid breaking reader trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools: dated scene list, calendar for the book's period, age chart, milestones chart. Spot checks: travel math, injury recovery windows, academic/fiscal calendars, tech availability. Mini exercise: echo early date anchors later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Audit and remove duplicate beats, scenes, or arguments to tighten the draft and target planned cuts (e.g., reduce by specific word counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print a scene/section list, write each purpose in five words, circle repeats, combine or cut. Example: keep one scene showing kindness instead of three; fold duplicate nonfiction chapters into one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open issues list
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a running list of plot holes, unanswered questions, missing bridges between ideas, research gaps, and permissions with status tags (fix now, research, park).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark owner and due dates. Example entries: 'Who paid for the lawyer in chapter 14' or 'Source for the 62 percent retention claim.' Finish the pass with a promise, beat sheet, and short issues list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene purpose check (G-F-C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every scene or chapter has a Goal, Friction, and Change (G, F, C). Blank boxes indicate a cut or rewrite needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction example: Goal — steal the file; Friction — security guard arrives; Change — thief leaves without file but learns a lead. Nonfiction: goal = teach a weekly planning method; friction = conflicting incentives; change = reader leaves with a checklist and warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrances and exits (start late, leave early)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open scenes late in the action and end them early once the beat is resolved or a hook is set; avoid extraneous arrivals/departures and routine detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings that work: mid-action, mid-thought, mid-argument. Endings that work: resolved beat or a hook (reveal, choice, clock). Quick fix for fiction: delete arrivals/parking/coffee orders; nonfiction: lead with a question, result, or number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition control
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid info-dumps: deliver context when readers need it, prefer action or dialogue for fact delivery, and use summary sparingly as a bridge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: keep background in bite sizes. Scan for paragraphs with more than three sentences of pure information and halve them or move part later. Use sidebars or figures in nonfiction for definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microtension on every page
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain small, page-level tension (a withheld detail, a question, a mismatch between words and body language) to keep curiosity and drive forward momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools: a question in narration, sensory mismatches, nearby deadlines. Nonfiction: a test, counterexample, or trade-off. Mini exercise: add one microtension device to every page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid monotony by varying scene/chapter lengths and modes (dialogue, action, reflection, summary) to maintain reader attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern ideas: three quick beats then a longer scene, dense analysis followed by Q&A. Mini exercise: label scenes S/M/L and avoid long runs of one size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions and bridges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear bridges to signal shifts in time, place, topic, or POV to prevent reader whiplash; tie endings to the next chapter's question or beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction moves: end a scene with a choice that implies the next location; anchor POV shifts in first line. Nonfiction: close sections by naming the next question and use subheads that label steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual accessibility and formatting for skimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Format pages for easy skimming with short paragraphs, regular subheads, bulleted lists, white space and figures/tables where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot check: open to a random page—if it looks like a wall of text, add subheads and break paragraphs. In nonfiction, use tables for data rather than burying it in prose; reformat a dense chapter for a busy commuter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the lead has a clear desire, hard obstacles, and meaningful choices with consequences; avoid resolution by lucky coincidence or offstage expert fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction check: list three decisions the lead makes in the first third; if two are reactions, redesign. Nonfiction version: define the reader's goal, state friction, and offer options with trade-offs rather than a single silver-bullet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonistic forces with credible motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Give opposition shape—person, system, or self—with a logic that holds; let the antagonist's reasons feel human, systemic, or psychological rather than pure evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: write a paragraph from the antagonist's perspective to clarify motive, then show an action that demonstrates that motive before the midpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast design (each named character has a job)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a clear role/function to every named character (mentor, foil, skeptic, enabler, witness) and ensure no duplicates; give depth beyond tokenism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tool: index cards with name, function, and one beat of growth. Merge or drop duplicates. Nonfiction: treat concepts and sources as a cast with unique functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV strategy and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick viewpoint, tense, and psychic distance and hold them; use one viewpoint per scene and signal shifts clearly; map multi-POV rotations to avoid leaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: first person for intimacy, close third for focus, distant third for scope. Signal time jumps (yesterday, three months later). Exercise: circle thought-words and check whether they leak across heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interiority and dialogue (show through action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blend thought, feeling, and action; ensure dialogue carries subtext and moves the scene rather than recapping backstory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer body language to tags; avoid on-the-nose exposition in dialogue. Exercise: mark places where dialogue explains backstory and move facts into action or objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and tone consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustain a consistent voice (authorial fingerprint) and tone appropriate to the audience, and avoid clichés, mixed metaphors, and inconsistent rhetorical posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vocabulary and sentence length to match expectations. Test: read a page aloud to hear rhythm; use a mini style sheet for profanity/jargon limits and tone notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction stance (role clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare and maintain a page-level stance (expert, guide, or peer) and honor its limits—use evidence for expert stance, steps and examples for guide, and honest experience for peer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag ethics: include disclaimers for health/legal/financial topics; change identifying details in client stories and state so; open each chapter with a promise and close with next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of the world (worldbuilding constraints and consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set explicit rules for the world (magic, tech, economy) early, show costs for breaking them, and pay off those constraints in the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: list three core rules, a visible cost, a loophole, and consequence for abuse. Place a consequence on the page before the midpoint to maintain plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting as function (use place to shape choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use setting details that affect choices and mood—sensory specifics that block or enable actions—rather than generic décor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick pass: cut generic weather, replace vague décor with a telling object. Nonfiction: use location to teach (warehouse walkthrough for supply chain). Exercise: write two lines on how setting blocks the easy path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity bible and tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a continuity bible (spreadsheet) logging items: item, first seen, description/rule, later reference, status, plus a timeline for dates, travel, sleep, and milestones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit trick: highlight every number (distances, prices, scores, dates) and verify. Log spelling choices and hyphenation for recurring terms. Use the bible to prevent inconsistencies during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research accuracy and sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat sources as load-bearing: quote originals, record full citation details, keep permissions list, and flag uncertainties with TK for follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circle stats and claims of 'first' or 'best' and find two independent sources with clear methods. If methods are weak, qualify or drop the claim. Store permission forms for quotes/epigraphs and check trademark usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural representation and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray people with depth and agency, avoid caricature and phonetic accents, hire and pay sensitivity readers where relevant, and anonymize or get consent for nonfiction case studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist: does representation go beyond food/clothes/trauma? Do characters from a group disagree with each other? For nonfiction, get consent and document approvals; share risky quotes with sources before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility checks (real-world constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify real-world intersections—travel times, injuries and recovery, legal/procedural details, professional constraints—to maintain plausibility where story meets reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System: make five rows — time, distance, money, medicine, law — and note one-line plausibility notes for major beats. Fix by researching, inserting a workaround with consequences, or changing the beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk flags (libel, privacy, dangerous how‑to)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and mitigate legal and ethical risks: libel/privacy concerns, medical/legal/financial advice requiring disclaimers, dangerous how-to steps, and permissions/releases for interviews or images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change names where appropriate but know that change alone may not remove risk. For high-stakes material, consult a lawyer or subject expert and budget time for approvals and releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre conventions and wordcount norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Match or intentionally signal deviations from category promises and wordcount norms so reader and seller expectations are met (e.g., romance 70–90k, fantasy 90–120k, business 50–75k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick test: list three must-haves for your category and tag scenes/chapters that deliver each promise. Note deliberate deviations and signal those early in text or jacket copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique value proposition / hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in one breath why a reader would choose this book—emotional payoff for fiction or specific skills/outcomes for nonfiction—and sharpen the back-of-book promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates: Fiction: 'When [protagonist] faces [problem] in [setting], failure costs [stakes], so [key choice] must land.' Nonfiction: 'For readers who want [outcome], this book offers [approach] through [method], leading to [result].' Test the hook with a reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive landscape and comps analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose 3–5 comps from the last five years with similar audience/category/vibe; document what aligns and where your book differs to inform positioning and possible content adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write two sentences per comp: what aligns and where you diverge. Use comp analysis to add missing elements (case studies, visuals) or adjust voice/format to cover gaps in the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader journey mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Map the reader's arc: promise in chapter one, escalation mid-book, decision near the end that honors setup, and appropriate emotional aftertaste or learning consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five-minute audit: write first and last sentence of each chapter in a column to scan for build. For nonfiction, ensure each chapter solves one problem and include recaps/exercises where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut, deepen, merge prioritisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Triage revision tasks into Keep & polish, Deepen (high-value moments), Merge (overlapping beats), and Cut (material that doesn't serve promise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridge work: list three foreshadowing seeds for payoff moments, add echoes of core motifs every three chapters, and insert one-line beats where leaps feel abrupt. Use color-coding or letter codes for the triage board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritised to-do list and sprint planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Order tasks by impact with columns for task, driver (promise/stakes/clarity), scope (pages/chapters), owner and date; run short sprints focused on big rocks first and prose later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example two-week sprint: two structural changes + two deepens, three short sessions per week for prose cleanup, and one weekly review to adjust scope. Keep a changelog with version names and dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta reader management and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Use early readers only after major structural choices settle; brief beta readers with hook, target reader, and three focus questions; request page-numbered comments rather than line edits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After beta: collate patterns, ignore single outliers unless they align with gut, run one more developmental pass for big fixes, then move to line edit and copyedit. Provide beta readers with a response form and focus questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission materials and packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare query materials and proposal aligned with the revised manuscript: fiction query (hook, category, word count, comps, mini-synopsis, bio); nonfiction proposal (overview, market, bio, chapter outline, sample chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep synopsis chronological with major turns and real ending. Update pitch after major revision: sharpen hook, align chapter summaries with revised order, and ensure accurate word count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working-file and editorial-deliverables negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree contractually on deliverables (editorial letter, margin notes/Track Changes, style sheet), timeline, fee structure, deposit, recheck scope, and whether a paid sample edit will be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample request message template provided. Clarifying these terms in writing prevents scope creep and ensures strategic direction plus concrete examples for actionable revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklists at multiple levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short diagnostic checklists at structure, pacing, character/voice, worldbuilding, market fit and revision planning stages to quickly surface problem areas and confirm readiness for next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout the guide: 'Does your lead drive action through choices with cost?' 'Do rules exist with costs for breaking them and do those costs hit the page?' 'Do genre promises appear on the page with matching word count?' Use these as quick gates before line editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for legal/ethical review where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag chapters or materials that may require legal review (libel/privacy) or subject-expert review (medical/legal/financial content), obtain permissions and releases, and include appropriate disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stakes feel high, bring in a lawyer or subject expert and budget time. Keep written approvals on file for interviews, images, and private materials; anonymize where needed and document consent.
